More recently, the SENSE projection model learned to predict all 11 Lancaster sensorimotor dimensions from lexical embeddings (Gupta et al., 2026), and embedding projection has shown practical value alongside LLM ratings in multilingual semantic-norm prediction (Peng et al., 2025). These results do not imply that distributional structure is equivalent to human semantic representation. They do show that properties expressed in human ratings can be statistically recoverable from linguistic distributions, making embeddings a substantive alternative for norm extension rather than merely a conventional computational baseline.

Prompting and embedding regression convert linguistic evidence into a rating in different ways. Prompting conditions a generative model on a verbal definition of the judgment and asks it to place a word on a response scale. Its principal advantage is that it does not require labeled examples from the target norm. Embedding regression does not interpret the norming instruction directly. It uses human-labeled words to learn which dimensions of a distributional space predict the requested rating, making its supervision explicit and construct-specific. Differences between their correlations with human judgments can therefore reflect representation, supervision, task interpretation, calibration, or readout. The relevant comparison is between complete estimation procedures, not a pure test of which underlying architecture "knows" more about a word. This distinction is especially important when the intended application is lexical extension, because partial human norms provide information that a zero-shot comparison would deliberately leave unused.

Correspondence depends not only on the property being rated but also on the vocabulary being estimated. Prior evaluations have used complete-case overlaps, concreteness-balanced samples, words passing familiarity or knownness thresholds, early-acquired vocabulary, translated concepts, and samples restricted or matched by part of speech (Green et al., 2025; Hagihara & Miyazawa, 2026; Kello et al., 2026; Martínez et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2025). These choices were appropriate to their respective questions, but they make construct comparisons conditional on different lexical samples. Frequency indexes exposure to a word, concreteness distinguishes abstract concepts from referents more readily characterized through sensory experience, and polysemy complicates isolated-word judgments because a type-level rating may privilege one sense or aggregate across uses (Hoffman et al., 2013; Reijnierse et al., 2019; Trott & Bergen, 2026). The words requiring norm extension need not resemble the familiar, concrete, well-attested items already represented in several databases.

Correlation also leaves two measurement questions unresolved. First, an estimator can preserve the ordering of words while using the response scale differently from human raters. Prior norming work has observed compressed or stretched LLM rating distributions (Hagihara & Miyazawa, 2026) and divergences between correlation and squared error (Peng et al., 2025); linear mappings have also been used more generally to align black-box model outputs with human judgments (Van Den Burg et al., 2025). Calibration must therefore be separated from rank-order correspondence before absolute-error differences are interpreted as lexical moderation. Second, two procedures can have different average performance while retaining nonredundant information about the human target. Hybrid human-LLM and model-ensemble research has shown the value of combining differently biased judgments (Abels & Lenaerts, 2025; Trott, 2024b), but complementarity between zero-shot norm ratings and supervised embedding estimates has received less attention. A combination analysis is informative here as a test of nonredundancy, not as a search for a winning benchmark system.

A constrained embedding readout provides a controlled conceptual bridge between zero-shot prompting and optimized regression. Semantic-projection methods recover human feature judgments by locating interpretable directions between opposing anchors in an embedding space (Grand et al., 2022). In the present progression, zero-shot LLM ratings define the judgment through instructions; a label-anchored BGE direction uses human ratings only to define contrasting prototypes; and BGE ridge regression uses continuous human ratings to optimize a predictive direction. The axis and ridge both project BGE representations, but they differ in how supervision determines that projection. The progression tests how correspondence changes as human labels specify the target more directly; it does not localize information inside an LLM. The present study evaluates these procedures across 18 psycholinguistic dimensions and one common 1,636-word holdout. Six LLMs (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o mini, Claude Haiku 4.5, GPT-5.4, Claude Sonnet 5, and Gemini 3.6 Flash) supply instruction-defined zero-shot judgments. Label-anchored BGE projection supplies a prototype-defined readout, and supervised GloVe and BGE regression supply continuously optimized predictions trained on 4,913 labeled words. We ask whether correspondence depends on the target construct, whether the six LLMs share a recurrent construct profile, how the controlled readout progression changes performance, how much apparent lexical moderation reflects scale calibration, and whether instruction-defined and label-optimized estimates retain complementary information. Human disagreement is retained as a descriptive robustness analysis rather than an organizing claim.

2. Method

>Method

2.1 Norm dimensions

The analysis included 18 psycholinguistic dimensions drawn from six published norm sets. Eleven dimensions came from the Lancaster Sensorimotor Norms (Lynott et al., 2020): six perceptual dimensions (auditory, visual, haptic, interoceptive, gustatory, and olfactory) and five action-effector dimensions (foot/leg, hand/arm, head, mouth, and torso), each rated from 0 to 5. Valence, arousal, and dominance came from Warriner et al. (2013) and were rated from 1 to 9. The remaining dimensions were concreteness (Brysbaert et al., 2014; 1-5), socialness (Diveica et al., 2023; 1-7), iconicity (Winter et al., 2024; 1-7), and age of acquisition (Kuperman et al., 2012; 1-25). The set was selected to span sensorimotor, affective, and lexical judgments while retaining enough common vocabulary to evaluate every estimator on one holdout sample.

Where overlapping constructs were available, we prioritized norm sets oriented toward American English. We therefore did not include the Glasgow Norms (Scott et al., 2019), which were collected from native English speakers recruited from the University of Glasgow community. Four of the included resources explicitly sampled US residents or American English speakers, whereas the Lancaster norms required English as a first language and used American spellings but did not report participant location. The socialness norms required English fluency but likewise did not report participant location and included both first-and additional-language speakers. Excluding the Glasgow Norms therefore reduced one known source of cross-dimension population heterogeneity, although it did not make the rater populations uniform.

Several dimensions have strongly non-normal distributions. Gustatory and olfactory ratings, in particular, are concentrated near the bottom of their scales, with a smaller set of words receiving substantial ratings. Correlations for these dimensions consequently reflect, in part, discrimination between the large group near the floor and the smaller group above it. We retain Pearson correlations because they measure the correspondence relevant to extending the published mean ratings, but interpret results for floor-concentrated dimensions with this distributional feature in mind.

2.2 Vocabulary and sampling

The final eligible vocabulary comprised 6,549 single-word entries that had ratings on all 18 dimensions and a GloVe embedding. Requiring complete data across six norm sets created a common basis for estimator and construct comparisons, but also restricted the vocabulary. The abstract-concrete range was well represented, whereas the genuinely low-frequency and late-acquired tails were truncated by the overlap among source norms. The sample should therefore be understood as representing the lexical range covered jointly by the included norms, not the English lexicon in full.

Words were stratified jointly by concreteness quintile, Zipf-frequency tertile, and WordNet polysemy band (1, 2-3, 4-9, or 10 or more synsets; Miller, 1995). A 25% holdout target was allocated proportionally across the 58 occupied cells and sampled within cell, ensuring deliberate representation across the observed concreteness, frequency, and polysemy ranges. The fixed holdout contained 1,636 words and the training set contained 4,913.

The holdout had a mean concreteness rating of 3.13 (SD = 1.00, range = 1.19-5.00), mean SUBTLEX-US Zipf frequency of 3.49 (SD = 0.67, range = 2.47-6.50; SUBTLEX-US: Brysbaert & New, 2009; Zipf scale: Van Heuven et al., 2014), and mean WordNet synset count of 3.77 (SD = 4.18, range = 1-75). Polysemy was represented by the number of WordNet synsets and log-transformed in the moderation analyses. Holdout words were not used to fit the embedding regressions or select the labeled prototypes used in the axis analysis.

2.3 Zero-shot LLM ratings

Ratings were collected from six proprietary models spanning three providers: GPT-4.1, GPT-4o mini, and GPT-5.4 (OpenAI); Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 5 (Anthropic); and Gemini 3.6 Flash (Google). The archived API identifiers and run records are provided in the model registry included with the accompanying reproducibility materials. The original model runs were collected in June and August 2026. Four dimensions were recollected for every model in October 2026 as described below; the analyzed records combine the unaffected dimensions from the original runs with those replacements.

Each word-dimension pair was submitted as a separate single-turn request. Prompts combined standardized, LLM-adapted instructions from the corresponding human norming task with the target word on a new line, and the wording was held constant across models. A prompt audit found that the original head, interoceptive, mouth, and torso templates included example actions while the other templates did not. Those four dimensions were therefore rerun for all six models without the examples, and only the uniform-prompt replacements enter the analyses. For example, the dominance prompt was: Rate the sense of control this word evokes. Range: 1-9 (1 = controlled/submissive,9 = in control/dominant). Reply with one number.

Word: triumph Models were instructed to return only an integer on the original response scale. GPT-4.1, GPT-4o mini, Claude Haiku 4.5, and GPT-5.4 were queried at temperature 0; reasoning was disabled for GPT-5.4. Claude Sonnet 5 does not accept non-default temperature settings, so thinking was disabled and effort set to low. Gemini 3.6 Flash was run at its default temperature and minimal supported thinking level. Output limits were set only to permit the requested short integer response.

All analyses use each model's single returned integer response, providing one common scoring rule across model families. When token probabilities are available, integer responses can instead be summarized as a probability-weighted expected value, which has produced modest improvements over the most probable response in prior work (Conde, Grandury, et al., 2026; Martínez et al., 2025). Expected-value scoring was not used here because token probabilities were not uniformly exposed across the evaluated models and because this refinement does not address the present comparison across constructs and lexical samples.

Each model was expected to produce 29,448 ratings (1,636 words × 18 dimensions). Each analyzed word-dimension pair was queried once per model; the study therefore does not estimate within-model test-retest reliability. Four historical Gemini responses outside the rerun dimensions could not be parsed as valid integers and were retained as missing. All other analyzed responses were valid; analyses used pairwise-complete observations where necessary.

2.4 Embedding regression

Two embedding spaces were evaluated. GloVe2024 is a 300-dimensional static distributional model trained on 2024 Wikipedia and Gigaword 5 (Carlson et al., 2025). BGE-large-en-v1.5 is a 1,024dimensional transformer encoder trained with contrastive objectives (Xiao et al., 2023). Each BGE input was the isolated bare word, with no instruction prefix; vectors used the model's default CLS pooling and were normalized to unit length. The pair was intended to represent a classical static embedding and a strong contemporary encoder, not to identify the best embedding space available.

A separate ridge regression was fitted for each combination of embedding space and norm dimension. Models were trained on the 4,913 labeled training words and evaluated on the fixed holdout. Ridge models were fitted with glmnet using an elastic-net mixing parameter of α = 0; the penalty parameter λ was selected by five-fold cross-validation using mean squared error and the minimum-error value of λ (Friedman et al., 2010). No holdout ratings contributed to model fitting or penalty selection.

2.5 Label-anchored embedding axis

The label-anchored analysis assessed how much predictive performance could be obtained from a constrained direction in BGE space without fitting regression coefficients. For each dimension, the lower and upper 20% empirical quantiles of the training ratings defined opposing prototype sets. Quantiles used the observed-value rule (type 1), and every word tied at either boundary was retained. The mean normalized vector of the lower prototype set was subtracted from the corresponding upper-set mean, and the resulting direction was normalized. Each holdout word received a score equal to the dot product of its normalized BGE vector with that direction. Ten-percent and 25% tails were specified as sensitivity checks. This procedure uses supervision: labels from the full training pool determine which words define the two poles. It differs from ridge regression in that it estimates no continuous mapping from embeddings to ratings and fits no regression coefficients. It is therefore model-light but not label-light: its practical advantage is computational simplicity, not a demonstrated reduction in the number of human labels required.

2.6 Statistical analyses

For every estimator and dimension, predictions were compared with human mean ratings using Pearson's r across the holdout words. Mean correlations summarize performance across the 18 dimensions, but the construct-specific estimates are the primary comparison. Agreement among the dimension profiles of the six LLMs was assessed with Kendall's coefficient of concordance, pairwise Spearman correlations of within-model dimension ranks, and a Friedman test.

Gemini 3.6 Flash, the LLM with the highest mean holdout correlation, was used for focused comparisons with BGE. Because the same holdout was used both to select Gemini and to compare it with BGE, the resulting intervals and p values do not incorporate uncertainty from model selection and apply only to the evaluated model panel. Per-dimension differences between Gemini and BGE correlations were evaluated by paired bootstrap resampling of words within dimension (2,000 resamples). Each resample scored the two estimators on the same words, and percentile intervals were calculated for the difference r BGE -r Gemini . Two-sided bootstrap p values were adjusted across the 18 dimensions using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure.

Correlation asks whether an estimator orders words similarly to human raters; calibration asks whether it also uses the human response scale accurately. Scale calibration was evaluated with scale-normalized mean absolute error (MAE): the absolute difference between predicted and human ratings divided by the response-scale span. For Gemini and the mean of the six LLM ratings, a dimension-specific linear mapping from model ratings to human means was estimated out of fold. The same deterministic ten-fold assignment was used across dimensions, with words stratified by the existing concreteness × frequency × polysemy cells. Each fold was predicted from a regression fitted on the other nine folds, so every recalibrated value was generated without using that word's human rating. Recalibration is therefore supervised by labeled holdout words, although out-of-fold prediction prevents evaluation on the same observations used to fit each mapping.

Lexical moderation was analyzed first on raw Gemini and BGE scale-normalized absolute errors and then after out-of-fold Gemini recalibration. Mixed-effects models included standardized concreteness, Zipf frequency, and log WordNet synset count and their interactions with estimator. The supported random-effects structure included a word intercept and uncorrelated intercept and estimator slope terms by dimension (Bates et al., 2015). Models were estimated by maximum likelihood, and the contribution of the interactions was tested against reduced models. As a calibration-invariant check, Pearson correlations were also calculated within each concreteness quintile for 17 dimensions, excluding concreteness itself because the quintiles restrict its range. A word bootstrap compared the mean BGE-minus-LLM correlation gap between the most abstract and most concrete quintiles.

Complementarity was tested using the mean of the six LLM ratings rather than the post-selected Gemini series. The question was whether the two procedures made partly different errors-that is, whether each retained information about the human ratings that the other missed. Within each dimension, ten-fold cross-fitting estimated human rating ~LLM mean + BGE and generated predictions for held-out folds. The LLM-only and BGE-only comparators were passed through the same foldwise linear procedure. The analysis was repeated over 20 stratified fold assignments. Because all coefficients were learned within the evaluation holdout, the combined correlation is a descriptive test of nonredundancy rather than an external estimate of deployable performance. A second, outcome-free check standardized each prediction series using its own within-dimension mean and standard deviation, then averaged the two series with fixed 50/50 weights. This standardization and weighting used no human ratings; human outcomes were used only to evaluate the resulting combination.

For each dimension, human disagreement was calculated over the 1,636 holdout words from itemlevel rating standard deviations in the source norms and divided by the dimension's scale span. Associations with performance were examined across the 18 heterogeneous dimensions and treated as descriptive robustness checks. Reliability of the human item means was estimated as the variance of item means minus the mean sampling-error variance (item SD squared divided by its number of raters), divided by the variance of item means. We also repeated the association without three influential dimensions: gustatory and olfactory ratings were strongly floor-concentrated, whereas age of acquisition used a 1-25 nominal scale that substantially exceeded its observed holdout range. These checks assessed whether mean item SD supported a general estimator contrast.

For the label-anchored analysis, holdout correlations for the axis, Gemini, the six-LLM mean, and BGE ridge were compared by paired word bootstrap within dimension (2,000 resamples), with Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment separately for each comparator. All analyses were conducted in R; the main build records the complete model registry, validation checks, code, generated tables, and retained diagnostics.

3. Results

>Results

3.1 Performance across norm dimensions

Performance differed substantially across estimators and norm dimensions. BGE had the highest mean holdout correlation across the 18 dimensions (M r = .734), followed by the six-LLM mean (M r = .685), GloVe (M r = .652), and Gemini 3.6 Flash (M r = .640). Mean performance among the LLMs ranged from .565 for Claude Haiku 4.5 to .640 for Gemini (Table 1). Averaging the six LLM ratings raised mean LLM correspondence to .685. These averages summarize the evaluated procedures; the central result is the variation across constructs. The comparison did not reduce to a simple contrast between broad norm classes. BGE led on dominance despite the strong LLM results for valence and arousal, and it led on four of the six sensory dimensions despite LLM advantages for gustatory and olfactory strength. Figure 1 shows the correlations for every estimator, with the six LLMs summarized as a range. The focused comparison between Gemini and BGE supported the same pattern. After Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment, BGE was distinguished from Gemini on 12 dimensions and Gemini was distinguished from BGE on four: age of acquisition, arousal, olfactory strength, and valence. Concreteness and gustatory strength were not distinguished. The largest BGE advantages appeared for head (∆r = .419), dominance (∆r = .326), auditory strength (∆r = .311), and torso (∆r = .218); Gemini's largest advantage was for age of acquisition (∆r = -.127).

Table 2 shows how estimator differences appear at the top of the scale, listing the five highest-scoring holdout words under human ratings, the six-LLM average, and BGE ridge. The six dimensions include the largest BGE advantages (head, dominance), dimensions where LLM ratings were strong (olfactory, valence, age of acquisition), and iconicity, which was weak for every estimator. For head involvement, the words rated highest by human raters largely involved perception through the head (smell, hear, sniff ), whereas the six-LLM average favored head movement and posture (dizzy, prostrate, flinch). For dominance, human raters placed win, self, and successful at the top of the scale, whereas the six-LLM average favored words denoting power over others (supremacy, conquer, annihilate). Where LLM correspondence was strong, as for olfactory strength, the top lists overlapped more closely (fragrant, smell). BGE's top words diverged from the human lists in a different way: for head and dominance, it favored mental and evaluative words (cognitive, mental; virtuous, excellence), so its correlation advantage on these dimensions did not show up as a closer match at the top of the scale.

3.2 Consistency across LLMs

Although the LLMs differed in mean performance, their dimension profiles were highly similar. Kendall's coefficient of concordance across the six within-model rankings was W = .945, Friedman χ2(17) = 96.43, p < .001. Pairwise Spearman correlations between dimension rankings ranged from .853 to .988, with a mean of .935. The common profile is visible in Figure 2: valence, concreteness, and age of acquisition generally ranked near the top, and gustatory strength ranked between second and sixth for every model; head involvement and dominance generally ranked near the bottom. The main exception was GPT-4o mini, which ranked dominance 12th but iconicity 18th. The models were therefore not interchangeable in absolute performance, but construct-level strengths and weaknesses recurred across the evaluated panel.

3.3 A controlled progression of readouts

The prototype-defined BGE axis provided an intermediate readout between instruction-defined LLM judgment and continuously optimized ridge regression. Its mean holdout correlation was .624. BGE ridge exceeded the axis on all 18 dimensions, showing the value of using continuous training ratings to optimize the projection direction. The constrained axis had reliably higher correlations than Gemini on six dimensions after the paired-bootstrap tests were adjusted for multiple comparisons: auditory, interoceptive, foot/leg, head, torso, and dominance. Gemini was reliably higher on 10: visual, haptic, gustatory, olfactory, hand/arm, valence, arousal, socialness, age of acquisition, and concreteness; mouth and iconicity did not differ reliably. Relative to the six-LLM mean, the axis was reliably higher on four of these dimensions (auditory, head, torso, and dominance) and reliably lower on 12; interoceptive and foot/leg did not differ reliably. Figure 3 shows these paired differences against Gemini and the six-LLM mean. The axis correlated strongly with valence (.801), concreteness (.800), and socialness (.749), even though Gemini remained stronger on each. Results were reasonably stable across the prespecified prototype widths: the median range across the 10%, 20%, and 25% tail rules was .013, and the largest range was .088 for gustatory strength.

3.4 Calibration and lexical composition

Raw absolute-error differences were dominated by scale use. Mean scale-normalized MAE was .170 for Gemini, .133 for the six-LLM mean, and .084 for BGE. After dimension-specific out-of-fold linear recalibration, the corresponding LLM values fell to .093 and .088, while BGE remained .084. Thus, the raw Gemini-BGE MAE gap of approximately .086 narrowed to .009. BGE retained lower recalibrated MAE than Gemini on 13 dimensions and than the recalibrated six-LLM mean on 10, but the large raw error contrast did not primarily reflect rank-order failure. Figure 4 shows this convergence by dimension. The same distinction changed the lexical-moderation result. With raw Gemini ratings, BGE had lower error at the mean of the lexical predictors (b = -.0857, t = -4.61), and the three estimator interactions improved fit, χ2(3) = 232.15, p < .001. The BGE-by-concreteness interaction was positive (b = .0116), χ2(1) = 211.34, p < .001, apparently indicating a larger BGE advantage for abstract words. Raw BGE advantages were also larger for more frequent words (b = -.0048, χ2(1) = 28.24) and smaller for more polysemous words (b = .0044, χ2(1) = 22.87). After out-of-fold Gemini recalibration, however, the interactions disappeared jointly, χ2(3) = .71, p = .870, as did the concreteness interaction, χ2(1) = .11, p = .739. The raw frequency and polysemy interactions likewise did not survive recalibration. These effects therefore described differences in response-scale use, not stable lexical moderation of relative correspondence.

The calibration-invariant within-quintile analysis provided more limited evidence. Across 17 dimensions, the mean BGE-minus-Gemini correlation gap was .061 larger in the most abstract than the most concrete quintile (95% bootstrap interval [.022, .106]). For the six-LLM mean, the corresponding difference was .027 [-.008, .061]. The result supports a modest concreteness-related difference for Gemini within this restricted vocabulary, but not the broader claim that embedding regression generally gains its advantage on abstract words.

3.5 Complementarity of instruction-and label-defined estimates

Cross-fitted combination supported nonredundancy between the six-LLM mean and BGE: when one procedure missed some human-rating variation, the other often retained part of it. Under the same foldwise linear procedure, the single-component predictions averaged .684 for the LLM mean and .733 for BGE, and their combined prediction averaged .789. These component values differ slightly from the raw correlations of .685 and .734 because the cross-fitted comparison passed every component through a foldwise linear fit. The mean gain over the stronger cross-fitted component was .028 and was positive on all 18 dimensions. Across 20 alternative stratified fold assignments, the gain varied by less than .002 within every dimension. Because the combination weights were learned within the evaluation holdout, these values describe complementarity in the present data rather than externally validated performance.

The outcome-free check reached the same qualitative conclusion more conservatively. A fixed 50/50 average of standardized LLM-mean and BGE predictions had a mean correlation of .774 and exceeded the stronger component descriptively on 13 of 18 dimensions. It reduced performance where the components were especially imbalanced, including head, dominance, and age of acquisition. A fixed average is therefore not a universally useful estimator, but its gains across most dimensions corroborate that instruction-defined and label-optimized procedures retain different predictive variation.

3.6 Human disagreement as a robustness check

Following Kello et al. (2026), we related scale-normalized mean item SD to estimator correspondence, while treating reliability of the item means as a distinct quantity. Human disagreement was associated with lower Gemini correspondence across dimensions (r = -.619, p = .006) and lower mean LLM correspondence (r = -.613, p = .007); its association with BGE was weaker (r = -.300, p = .227). This pattern did not support a general contrast in sensitivity to disagreement. Excluding gustatory, olfactory, and age of acquisition weakened the Gemini association to r = -.481, p = .070. Across all 18 dimensions, estimated reliability of the human item means tracked BGE performance more strongly (r = .881) than Gemini performance (r = .704). Disagreement is therefore retained as a qualification about the source measurements, not evidence that BGE is less affected by human uncertainty.

4. Discussion

>Discussion

4.1 Automated norms as construct-dependent measurements

The central result is not simply that BGE regression attained a higher average correlation than direct prompting. Correspondence depended on the construct and on how its target was specified. LLM ratings led for valence, arousal, gustatory strength, olfactory strength, and age of acquisition, whereas BGE regression led across most sensory and all effector dimensions. GloVe also exceeded every individual LLM in mean correlation, showing that the result was not limited to one contemporary encoder. An automated norm should therefore be understood as the output of a particular measurement procedure, not as an estimator-independent readout of a lexical property.

The dimension pattern broadly converges with prior LLM-rating studies while changing how that pattern should be interpreted. Xu et al. (2025) reported decreasing LLM-human correspondence from non-sensorimotor to sensory and motor properties, and Kello et al. (2026) likewise found substantial differences between psycholinguistic, perceptual, and action-effector judgments. The present results reproduce the relative difficulty of many effector judgments across a broader panel of current models. They also show that a supervised embedding procedure can correspond closely with human ratings for the same held-out words. Weak correspondence between zero-shot LLM ratings and human judgments is therefore not equivalent to evidence that a property cannot be estimated from linguistic representations. It may instead indicate that zero-shot scalar elicitation is a less effective measurement procedure for that judgment when partial human norms are available.

At the same time, this broad progression from non-sensorimotor to sensory to motor properties does not fully characterize performance across dimensions. Dominance illustrates the problem. Although dominance is collected alongside valence and arousal as an affective dimension, its estimator profile differed sharply: LLM ratings were strong for valence and arousal, whereas BGE and the label-anchored axis were much stronger for dominance (Figures 1 and 3). Gustatory and olfactory strength provide the converse example. Both are sensory dimensions, yet LLM ratings were highly competitive. Broad construct classes summarize a recurring pattern, but they do not determine how well a particular judgment can be recovered. The instructions, response scale, lexical distribution, and estimator together define the measurement being evaluated.

The six LLMs showed very similar dimension rankings despite differences in their average performance and provider. This consistency shows that the profile recurred within the evaluated panel rather than appearing in only one tested model. It does not identify why the profile recurred. Shared regularities in training data, common difficulty in mapping isolated words onto rating scales, prompt interpretation, and the properties of the source norms could all contribute. The concordance therefore characterizes the tested elicitation regime; it should not be read directly as a measure of what the models represent internally. Whether the profile persists under other prompts, forms of supervision, or future models remains an empirical question.

4.2 What estimator differences do (and do not) reveal about lexical knowledge

One interpretation is that direct prompting benefits when ordinary language routinely expresses the target property as an explicit evaluation. Valence and arousal have familiar evaluative vocabularies, and everyday descriptions often state directly whether something has a noticeable taste or smell. This account fits evidence that contextual calibration improves LLM sensorimotor ratings (Kello et al., 2026) and that language models perform better on linguistically mediated odor judgments than on nonverbal perceptual similarity (Kurfalı et al., 2025). Age of acquisition offers a related case: its ratings reflect partially distinct properties including familiarity, word length, frequency, and imagery-concreteness (Clark & Paivio, 2004). An LLM could approximate the judgment by combining these correlated cues rather than recovering a unitary representation of when speakers learned each word. The present analyses do not identify which cues the models used.

Embedding regression implements a different measurement procedure. It does not require a property to be produced as an explicit scalar evaluation; it learns from associations distributed across the embedding dimensions and anchors them to observed human labels. Grounded-cognition accounts emphasize that human concepts draw on perceptual and action systems (Barsalou, 1999 (Barsalou, , 2008)), but experiential properties also leave traces in linguistic structure (Andrews et al., 2009; Banks et al., 2021). Those traces may support supervised prediction even when a direct rating task is relatively ineffective. The result therefore concerns the effectiveness of supervised estimation from linguistic structure, not the source or grounding of that structure.

The label-anchored results sharpen this measurement point without resolving the mechanism. They extend semantic-projection work showing that human feature judgments can be recovered by projecting word embeddings onto interpretable directions defined by opposing anchors (Grand et al., 2022). Here, the lower and upper training-rating prototypes defined a BGE direction that captured substantial held-out variation in dominance, auditory strength, head involvement, and several other dimensions. Because the axis fits no regression coefficients, BGE's largest advantages over Gemini did not depend on a continuously optimized mapping. Unlike projections defined directly by lexical antonyms, the prototypes used human ratings across the full training pool. The axis and ridge are both scalar projections of the same normalized BGE vectors: the axis uses a difference between prototype centroids, whereas ridge estimates a covariance-adjusted direction from the continuous labels. Ridge's advantage on all 18 dimensions therefore shows the value of the optimized readout, not access to a broader representation.

The full progression separates three ways of specifying the construct. Zero-shot prompting operationalizes it through instructions and scale anchors. The prototype axis adds categorical information about the low and high regions of the human measure. Ridge uses continuous labels to optimize correspondence with that measure. Target specification therefore became progressively more direct, but correspondence did not increase monotonically: the axis surpassed Gemini and the six-LLM mean for selected dimensions and remained weaker for others. The progression is conceptual rather than a claim that one method dominates every use case.

Complementarity provides an equally important qualification. The LLM mean and BGE did not merely differ in average accuracy; their combination preserved human-rating variation that neither component captured alone. The gain from cross-fitted learned weights was consistent across dimensions and fold assignments, and a fixed outcome-free combination improved on the stronger component for most dimensions. This pattern resembles broader findings that differently biased human and model judgments can be useful in combination (Abels & Lenaerts, 2025; Trott, 2024b).

The high concordance of the six LLM profiles also fits Abels and Lenaerts's warning that nominally diverse model crowds can retain correlated errors: averaging improved correspondence here without eliminating shared weak dimensions. Instruction-defined judgment and label-optimized projection are therefore not interchangeable, even when one has the higher average correlation.

4.3 Calibration and lexical scope

The calibration analysis changes the interpretation of absolute error. Raw LLM ratings often preserved the human ordering while using only part of the available scale or shifting its location.

A dimension-specific linear mapping removed most of Gemini's excess MAE without materially changing correlation. More generally, this result cautions against interpreting concreteness-related differences in raw absolute error, such as those reported by Trott (2024a), without first checking response-scale calibration. The prominent raw interactions with concreteness, frequency, and polysemy disappeared after the same out-of-fold recalibration. They should therefore not be interpreted as robust evidence that BGE's correspondence advantage grows for abstract, frequent, or less polysemous words.

The within-quintile correlations support a narrower result. Gemini showed a larger BGE correlation advantage in the most abstract than the most concrete quintile, whereas the corresponding contrast for the six-LLM mean was uncertain. Semantic diversity could contribute: abstract words occur across more variable contexts, isolated-word ratings can privilege dominant construals, and contextualized sensorimotor judgments vary across uses (Hoffman et al., 2013; Reijnierse et al., 2019; Trott & Bergen, 2026). Because the study did not manipulate context or identify favored senses, the result does not establish a general abstract-word advantage for embedding regression. It also applies only to the common norm-covered vocabulary, which excludes much of the genuinely low-frequency and late-acquired range.

4.4 Implications for norm construction and extension

The measurement framing changes what validation is required for norm construction and extension. Direct prompting can be deployed immediately for a completely new dimension because it requires no labeled training set. That convenience is substantial, but validity evidence from another dimension or vocabulary does not automatically transfer. LLM ratings should be checked against at least a targeted human validation sample drawn to represent the intended lexical population, consistent with recent practical recommendations for LLM-assisted norming (Conde, Grandury, et al., 2026). When a substantial partial human norm exists (4,913 training words per dimension in the present comparison), embedding regression becomes available and should be evaluated alongside zero-shot LLM ratings on the same held-out labeled words.

The present results offer validation priorities rather than immutable rules. Embedding regression deserves particular consideration for action-effector and other sensorimotor dimensions when a partial human norm is available. LLM ratings remain competitive for valence and arousal, gustatory and olfactory ratings, and age of acquisition. A prototype-defined direction provides a computationally lightweight supervised alternative, although the present study does not show that it reduces the number of human labels required. If downstream applications require accurate scale values rather than rank ordering alone, calibration must be validated directly. Combining LLM and embedding estimates can also be useful when the combination is validated on external data. Future improvements may come from larger models, supervised adaptation, or multimodal evidence, but each changes the estimation procedure in a different way. Task-specific fine-tuning can improve sensorimotor alignment, with gains depending on the learning objective (Wu et al., 2026). Multimodal learning can benefit visually grounded properties by adding perceptual information rather than improving prediction from text alone (Xu et al., 2025). The present cross-sectional results do not determine whether any of these developments will eliminate the weakest dimensions.

4.5 Limitations

The estimators differ in corpora, training objectives, representations, and supervision. Direct prompting requires no labeled examples from the target norm; ridge regression uses thousands of them; and the axis uses the same training pool to define its prototypes. The comparison reflects realistic measurement procedures with different resource requirements, not a controlled test that isolates one psychological or computational mechanism. The axis-versus-ridge comparison controls the BGE representation and changes the supervised projection rule, but comparisons with LLM prompting change representation, supervision, and readout together. The results therefore show that complete procedures differ, not exactly where information resides within an LLM or why a particular procedure succeeds.

Beyond this structural asymmetry, the zero-shot results are conditional on the prompts, API versions, and settings tested. Although deterministic or minimal-variability settings were used where supported, repeated API calls may not yield identical ratings, and within-model repeatability remains to be evaluated. Instructions were standardized rather than optimized separately for each model. The four templates containing example lists were rerun without them, but the prompts remain concise adaptations rather than verbatim reproductions of every human task; dominance and iconicity have the largest remaining departures. The results therefore describe a common elicitation protocol rather than each model's best possible prompt or an exact simulation of the original norming studies.

A separate set of limitations concerns the target vocabulary. Eligibility required complete ratings across all 18 dimensions and availability in the GloVe vocabulary, which excluded the rarest words and linked the sample to the coverage of the source norms. The findings therefore concern English single words within this common lexical range rather than the English lexicon as a whole. Although stratification preserved variation in concreteness, frequency, and polysemy within the eligible vocabulary, it could not restore the low-frequency and late-acquired tails excluded before sampling.

The human benchmarks introduce related population and temporal constraints. The source norms were collected under different recruitment protocols and vary in their documentation of rater geography, first-language status, and multilingualism. Ratings may also change over time. Clark and Paivio (2004), for example, found correlations of .803 between imagery ratings collected in the 1960s and in 2001-2002 and .852 between familiarity ratings collected in the 1970s and in 2001-2002; the newer familiarity ratings were generally higher. Although those constructs are not analyzed here, the comparison shows that lexical ratings can remain strongly correlated while shifting over time.

These population and temporal differences are difficult to separate from uncertainty about the models' training data. The LLMs were trained on broad, largely undisclosed mixtures of language whose geographic, demographic, and temporal composition cannot be established. Model-human differences may therefore reflect mismatches between the human benchmarks and the models' training data, as well as estimator performance.

A further asymmetry concerns possible LLM exposure to the published norm databases, an issue raised previously in work on LLM-generated psycholinguistic norms (Trott, 2024a). Because the models' training data are undisclosed, we cannot determine whether they encountered the published norms. If they did, partial reproduction of stored ratings could inflate apparent zero-shot performance. Yet exposure does not readily explain differences among dimensions from the same resource: LLMs led for valence and arousal in the Warriner et al. (2013) norms, whereas BGE had a large advantage for dominance. This contrast does not rule out memorization, whose effects may vary by dimension, but shared publication history cannot explain the full pattern. The comparison remains asymmetric because embedding regression uses human labels explicitly, whereas any LLM exposure is unknown.

Finally, the evaluation criteria impose their own limits. Pearson correlation evaluates relative correspondence, not response-scale calibration, while normalized MAE combines rank error with differences in location and scale. The out-of-fold recalibration analysis separates these quantities within the present holdout, but it uses labeled holdout words and is not a label-free correction.

The learned complementarity analysis likewise uses cross-fitting within this one sample rather than an external test set. The fixed combination avoids outcome-fitted weights but can perform poorly when component quality is imbalanced. Floor-concentrated dimensions can attain high correlations through successful separation of a small off-floor group, and inference from 18 heterogeneous, partly related dimensions remains limited. Human disagreement is only a descriptive robustness measure; neither its association with performance nor its absence establishes the validity of the norm scores.

5. Conclusion

Psycholinguistic norm estimation is not one prediction problem. Instruction-defined LLM judgments, prototype-defined embedding projections, and continuously optimized regression corresponded differently with human ratings across constructs. Continuous optimization against human labels produced the highest average correspondence, while the prototype axis remained competitive on selected constructs. The procedures also retained complementary predictive variation. Calibration explained most of the raw absolute-error and lexical-moderation differences, showing why correlation and scale accuracy must be evaluated separately. These results make automated norm extension a measurement problem rather than a model-ranking exercise. Estimates should be validated for their intended construct, lexical population, supervision regime, and use of the response scale rather than treated as interchangeable measures of lexical knowledge.
